title: HE WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE… AND THE CHURCH WAS PROUD OF IT.
paragraphs: HE WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE… AND THE CHURCH WAS PROUD OF IT.

One forbidden relationship. One shocking scandal. One ancient commandment that exposed a church’s dangerous misunderstanding of grace. And one question that still confronts Christianity today: What happens when the people who proclaim Jesus stop taking His holiness seriously?
There are sins people commit in darkness because they are terrified of being discovered.
And then there are sins so openly tolerated that nobody even bothers to hide them anymore.
The second kind may be more dangerous than we realize.
Because when a person sins and trembles, there may still be a conscience crying out for mercy.
But when an entire church learns to celebrate what God has forbidden, something has gone terribly wrong.
Imagine walking into a gathering of believers in the ancient city of Corinth.
People are praying. Someone is speaking about spiritual gifts. Others are discussing the wisdom of God. The name of Jesus Christ is being proclaimed.
Everything sounds spiritual.
Until you discover something happening among them.
A man is having a sexual relationship with his father's wife.
Not merely an accusation whispered by an enemy.
Not a private suspicion circulating through the congregation.
The apostle Paul has received a report about it.
And what makes the situation even more disturbing is not simply the man's behavior.
It is the church's response.
They are arrogant when they should be grieving.
They are boasting when they should be mourning.
They are acting as though their spiritual confidence somehow excuses their moral blindness.
And Paul writes words that must have landed like thunder.
"It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife." — 1 Corinthians 5:1, KJV
Read that again.
His father's wife.
Not his own wife.
His father's.
And suddenly, an ancient commandment from Leviticus becomes impossible to ignore.
"Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's wife: it is thy father's nakedness." — Leviticus 18:8, KJV
Why would God forbid this relationship so explicitly?
Why describe sexual relations with a father's wife as uncovering the father's nakedness?
Why did Paul treat this Corinthian scandal with such severity?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
What does a scandal from nearly two thousand years ago reveal about the compromises we sometimes defend in the name of grace?
Because this story is not merely about a man who crossed a sexual boundary.
It is about a church that forgot the difference between welcoming sinners and approving sin.
And if we read it carefully, we may discover that the warning is closer to our own lives than we want to admit.
To understand the commandment, we need to enter the world in which it was first spoken.
Israel had been delivered from Egypt. God was forming a covenant people who were not to imitate every practice of the surrounding nations.
Their worship, justice, relationships, and sexual conduct were all to reflect their belonging to Him.
Leviticus 18 addresses forbidden sexual relationships, including relationships within the family.
The Hebrew of Leviticus 18:8 reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא
ʿErvat ʾeshet-ʾavikha lo tegalleh; ʿervat ʾavikha hi.
A close translation is:
"You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness."

The expression עֶרְוָה (ʿervah), translated "nakedness," can refer to bodily nakedness or sexual exposure. In the prohibitions of Leviticus 18, the phrase "uncover nakedness" functions as a way of describing prohibited sexual intimacy.
This is not merely a command about accidentally seeing someone unclothed.
The context concerns sexual boundaries.
And the Hebrew phrase אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ (ʾeshet-ʾavikha) means "your father's wife."
That distinction matters.
The text does not restrict the prohibition to a man's biological mother. It includes a woman married to his father, such as a stepmother.
Leviticus 18:7 separately addresses the nakedness of one's father and mother. Verse 8 specifically addresses the father's wife.
The law protects a boundary within the family that must not be crossed.
And the final words are striking.
"It is your father's nakedness."

The language connects the father's wife to the father's marital relationship. Sexual access to her is not presented as an isolated private decision. It violates a relationship that the law treats as belonging within the father's marriage.
It is a violation of family boundaries, marital fidelity, and the order God established for His covenant people.
This does not mean a woman is merely her husband's property, or that her dignity depends on him.
Scripture presents human beings as created in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and marriage as a union involving both husband and wife (Genesis 2:24).
The command concerns the seriousness of sexual relationships within the family, not permission to diminish the woman involved.
And the prohibition is repeated elsewhere.
Deuteronomy 22:30 declares that a man must not take his father's wife.
Leviticus 20:11 treats sexual intercourse with a father's wife as a grave offense under Israel's covenant law.
These were not casual cultural preferences.
They were solemn moral boundaries within the life of ancient Israel.
But here is where the story becomes even more revealing.
Centuries later, the apostle Paul confronts essentially the same kind of relationship in a Christian congregation.
Not in Israel's wilderness.
Not under the administration of ancient Israel's civil penalties.
But inside a church that confesses Jesus Christ as Lord.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 5:1 contains the phrase:
γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν
gynaika tina tou patros echein
Literally, in context, it means "for someone to have his father's wife."
The verb ἔχειν (echein), "to have," appears here in a context describing an ongoing illicit sexual relationship.
Paul does not tell us every detail.
He does not explicitly identify the woman as the man's biological mother, nor does he establish whether the man's father was alive or whether the woman was still married to him.
The most natural reading is that she was his father's wife or stepmother.
But we should not invent details Scripture does not provide.
We do not know the man's name.
We do not know the woman's name.
We do not know how the relationship began.
We do not know what excuses were offered.
What we do know is that Paul regarded the situation as unmistakably immoral.
And we know that the congregation's response deeply troubled him.
"And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned..." — 1 Corinthians 5:2, KJV
That word "puffed up" is devastating.
In Greek, Paul uses a form of φυσιόω (physioō), meaning to become inflated or arrogant.
They were spiritually swollen with pride.
Their problem was not merely that someone among them had sinned.
Their problem was that they had failed to respond with appropriate grief.
Think about that.
A church can possess spiritual language and still lack spiritual discernment.
A congregation can celebrate its knowledge and overlook its disobedience.
People can become so impressed with their freedom that they forget the One who freed them.
And we need to be careful here.
Paul does not say the church should hate the man.
He does not command them to humiliate him publicly for entertainment.
He does not encourage gossip, cruelty, or self-righteousness.
He calls them to take sin seriously.
There is an enormous difference.
Because biblical holiness is not permission to become merciless.
And biblical mercy is not permission to call evil good.
Both errors can destroy people.
One crushes sinners beneath condemnation.
The other leaves sinners trapped in what is destroying them.
Jesus came to rescue us from both.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to live between those two extremes.
Maybe you grew up around religious people who knew how to condemn but never learned how to restore.
You made a mistake, and suddenly you were treated as though your entire life could be reduced to your worst decision.
You learned to hide your struggles.
To smile while breaking.
To say "I'm blessed" when you were barely surviving.
Or perhaps your experience was different.
Maybe you encountered people who told you that because God loves you, nothing in your life really needs to change.
They called every correction judgment.
Every boundary oppression.
Every call to repentance an attack on your freedom.
And for a while, that message felt comforting.
Until the thing you were defending began destroying your peace.
Because sometimes what we call freedom is simply bondage that has learned to speak beautifully.
And sometimes the most loving words God gives us are the ones that interrupt the direction we are heading.
Leviticus 18:8 is one of those interruptions.
It tells us that desire does not automatically make a relationship righteous.
That mutual attraction does not erase every moral boundary.
That secrecy does not transform wrongdoing into innocence.
And that something can feel powerful, intimate, and emotionally convincing while still violating God's design.
This is not an invitation to suspect every relationship or to shame people for their histories.
It is a reminder that God's commands are not rewritten by the intensity of our feelings.
And then Paul takes the matter further.
In 1 Corinthians 5:6, he asks:
"Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?"
In the immediate context, leaven illustrates the spreading influence of tolerated wrongdoing and the congregation's boasting.
Paul is concerned not only for the individual but for the spiritual integrity of the church.
A community teaches through what it celebrates.
It teaches through what it confronts.
And it teaches through what it knowingly refuses to address.
A church does not become loving by pretending that sin has no consequences.
Neither does it become holy by treating wounded people as disposable.
This is why Paul's instructions must be read carefully.
He directs the Corinthian congregation to remove the unrepentant man from its fellowship.
That is a serious act of church discipline.
But it is not a license for violence, harassment, public humiliation, or the abandonment of compassion.
Nor does Paul command Christians to impose the civil penalties of ancient Israel upon people.
He is addressing the responsibility of a Christian congregation toward a professing believer openly persisting in serious wrongdoing.
He even distinguishes between judging those within the church's fellowship and attempting to police everyone outside it (1 Corinthians 5:12–13).
And in 1 Corinthians 5:5, the purpose of the severe disciplinary action includes the hope that the man's spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.
Even in correction, the ultimate concern is not revenge.
It is salvation.
Not the satisfaction of exposing someone.
But the possibility of bringing someone back to truth.
That is a distinction the modern church desperately needs to remember.
Because we live in a world where exposing a person's failure can become entertainment.
A scandal appears online.
Screenshots circulate.
Names are dragged through conversations.
People who have never met the individuals involved become judges, prosecutors, and executioners.
And somewhere in the noise, the actual human soul disappears.
Paul's words do not justify that behavior.
Biblical correction must be governed by truth, justice, humility, and the hope of restoration.
And when abuse, coercion, or exploitation is involved, protecting victims and pursuing appropriate accountability must never be sacrificed to preserve a religious institution's reputation.
Grace does not require silence in the face of harm.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending consequences no longer exist.
Restoration does not mean automatically restoring someone to a position of trust or authority.
The Gospel calls us to truth and mercy together.
But there is another detail in this Corinthian scandal that we cannot overlook.
Paul does not stop at condemning the sin.
He points the congregation to Christ.
"For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." — 1 Corinthians 5:7, KJV
There it is.
The center of everything.
Jesus Christ.
Paul moves from the corruption of the congregation to the sacrifice of the Savior.
Why?
Because holiness without Christ becomes an impossible attempt at self-salvation.
And grace without Christ's transforming lordship becomes an empty excuse for remaining unchanged.
The Christian life begins and continues through Jesus.
His death is not permission to cherish the very sins from which He came to redeem us.
His resurrection is not merely a promise that we can survive death.
It is also the foundation of a new life in which sin no longer has the final claim upon us.
Paul expresses this truth elsewhere:
"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
Grace is not God's declaration that sin never mattered.
The cross reveals how seriously sin matters.
And how immeasurably God loves sinners.
At Calvary, we see both truths.
The holiness of God is not dismissed.
The mercy of God is not withheld.
Jesus gives Himself for the ungodly.
He bears our sins.
He opens the way for forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
Not because we were already clean.
But because we could never cleanse ourselves.
And that changes how we read the Corinthian scandal.
The man's sin was serious.
The congregation's arrogance was serious.
But neither reality placed the situation beyond the need for the Gospel.
The answer was not to redefine the sin until it became acceptable.
The answer was to return to the Savior whose grace calls sinners to repentance.
And here is something that should make every believer examine their heart.
It is possible to condemn the Corinthian man while quietly protecting a different sin in ourselves.
We may never enter the relationship described in Leviticus 18:8.
But we may become skilled at defending our own disobedience.
We call bitterness discernment.
We call revenge justice.
We call greed ambition.
We call pride confidence.
We call dishonesty survival.
We call lust harmless entertainment.
We call spiritual indifference a busy season.
And then we wonder why our hearts feel increasingly distant from God.

Not every struggle is evidence of rebellion. Temptation is not the same as consenting to sin. A believer who is fighting, confessing, seeking help, and returning to Christ is not in the same position as someone defiantly celebrating wrongdoing.
But we must be willing to ask ourselves a difficult question.
Am I bringing my struggles into the light, or am I demanding that God bless what I refuse to surrender?
That question can hurt.
Especially when the thing we are holding on to has become part of our identity.
Especially when repentance may cost us a relationship, an opportunity, an image, or a comfortable way of living.
Especially when we know what Scripture says but are afraid of what obedience might require.
And yet Jesus never calls us to surrender something sinful because He delights in our pain.
He calls us away from sin because He is Lord, because He loves us, and because life apart from His truth cannot give us the freedom we were created to enjoy.
There is another scene in the New Testament that helps us understand the heart of Christ.
In John 8, a woman accused of adultery is brought before Jesus.
Her accusers want to use her as a weapon in their confrontation with Him.
But Jesus refuses to turn her into a spectacle.
He exposes the hypocrisy of those who seek to condemn her.
And when the accusers have departed, He tells her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV
Those two statements belong together.
"Neither do I condemn thee."
"Go, and sin no more."
Mercy.
And a call to change.
Compassion.
And holiness.
Jesus does not deny the moral seriousness of adultery.
Neither does He allow the woman to be reduced to her accusation.

We should note that the account in John 7:53–8:11 has a well-known textual history: the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John do not contain it, and modern Bibles commonly mark the passage. Its themes should therefore be considered alongside securely attested passages about Jesus' mercy and His call to repentance.
And those themes are unmistakably present throughout the New Testament.
Jesus came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32).
He came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10).
And those who belong to Him are called to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4).
This is why the Gospel is greater than mere moral improvement.
Jesus does not simply hand us a list of rules and leave us alone to repair ourselves.
He offers reconciliation with God through His death and resurrection.
He calls us to repent and believe.
He gives His Spirit to His people.
He teaches us to walk in truth, even when the process is difficult and unfinished.
And sometimes that process begins with one sentence we have been terrified to say.
"Lord, I was wrong."
No excuse.
No performance.
No blaming everyone else.
Just truth.
Perhaps that is where someone reading this article is standing right now.
You love Jesus.
Or at least you want to.
But there is something you have been hiding.
A relationship you know is not right.
A secret habit you keep promising to abandon.
A lie that has grown so large you no longer know how to confess it.
A compromise you once resisted but now barely notice.
And the worst part is not that you have stopped hearing God's Word.
It is that you have become very good at explaining why it does not apply to you.
If that describes you, do not mistake conviction for hopelessness.
The fact that God's Word confronts you does not mean His mercy is unavailable.
Scripture says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice what the promise does not say.
It does not say we must pretend.
It does not say we must become perfect before approaching God.
It does not say we can purchase forgiveness through religious performance.
It calls us to confession and directs us to God's faithfulness.
The cleansing is His work.
The mercy is His gift.
And our response is to stop hiding and come into the light.
But what happened to the man in Corinth?
Did he repent?
Was he restored?
Did the church finally learn to mourn what it had previously tolerated?
Paul's later correspondence offers a possible glimpse of hope.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, he speaks about a person who has experienced discipline and urges the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward him, lest he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Some interpreters have connected this individual with the man in 1 Corinthians 5.
Others believe Paul is discussing a different offender and a separate incident.
The text does not identify the person clearly enough to settle the question.
We should not claim certainty where Scripture does not give it.
But one truth remains unmistakable.
Paul understood that discipline must not become endless punishment when repentance calls for forgiveness and comfort.
A church that refuses to confront serious wrongdoing fails in its responsibility.
A church that refuses to show mercy to the repentant also fails.
The Gospel demands more of us than either extreme.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes most personal.
Because some people reading this are not the person hiding the sin.
You are the person who has already confessed.
You have already walked away.
You have already suffered the consequences.
You have already cried over what you did.
But there are people who still introduce you by your worst chapter.
They remember the scandal.
They remember the failure.
They remember the version of you that existed before repentance.
And no matter how sincerely you seek Christ, they keep returning you to the place where you fell.
Hear this carefully.
Repentance does not erase every earthly consequence.
Trust may need to be rebuilt.
Relationships may not return to what they were.
Some wounds require years of healing, and some responsibilities may never appropriately be restored.
But your past does not possess greater authority than the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about people whose former lives included serious sins.
Then he declared:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
And such were some of you.
Not because their past had never happened.
Not because their wrongdoing was imaginary.
But because the grace of God had changed their standing and called them into a new way of life.
Those words carry astonishing hope.
The Gospel does not say that sin is harmless.
It says that Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
It does not say that consequences are meaningless.
It says that consequences do not have the power to cancel God's promises.
It does not say that Christians will never struggle again.
It says that those who belong to Christ are no longer defined solely by the bondage from which He is delivering them.
And this is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because the scandal was good.
Not because the damage was small.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus can redeem a life that sin has devastated.
He can bring truth into a house built on secrecy.
He can teach humility to a heart inflated with pride.
He can lead a compromised believer back to obedience.
He can comfort the wounded.
He can forgive the repentant.
He can form a new future where shame once seemed to have written the final sentence.
And this is why we must never preach grace as though it means God has stopped caring about holiness.
Real grace is more beautiful than that.
Grace welcomes us when we have nothing to boast about.
Grace tells the truth when we would rather hide.
Grace leads us to repentance when our hearts have wandered.
Grace sustains us when obedience feels costly.
And grace reminds us that the blood of Jesus is sufficient for every sinner who comes to Him in faith.
The Corinthian church needed that grace.
The man at the center of the scandal needed that grace.
And so do we.
Before you move on, ask yourself something.
If the Lord were to expose the one area of your life you most desperately want to keep hidden, would you run farther into darkness?
Or would you finally come to Him?

You do not have to publish your private sins for strangers to examine. You do not have to expose sensitive details in a public comment section. Genuine confession should be made wisely, with appropriate accountability, and with the safety of those affected in mind.
But you can stop pretending before God.
You can seek help from a trustworthy pastor, mature believer, or qualified professional where needed.
You can take the next honest step.
And you can remember that the Savior who calls you to repentance is the same Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
You do not need to share the details of your struggle. Those simple words may encourage someone else who thought they were fighting alone.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that repentance is possible.
That healing takes time.
That grace is real.
That Jesus has not stopped calling people home.
And if this article helped you understand why Leviticus 18:8 mattered, and why Paul's response in 1 Corinthians 5 was so serious, please save it.
Not merely because it is a powerful story.
But because there may come a day when you need to remember that God's holiness and God's mercy are not enemies.
One thoughtful share can bring Scripture into the life of someone who would never think to search for a Bible study.
Someone may be wrestling with a forbidden relationship.
Someone may be drowning in guilt.
Someone may have confused God's patience with His approval.
Someone may have been wounded by religious cruelty and needs to encounter the truth of Christ's compassion.
And someone may simply need to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Never use Scripture as a weapon to embarrass someone.
Let it become an invitation to encounter Jesus.
We are here to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ through biblical truth, repentance, grace, forgiveness, spiritual growth, and discipleship.
Not just through messages that comfort.
But also through passages that challenge us.
Because sometimes the verse we would rather avoid is the very passage God uses to bring us back to truth.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and reach more people, there is another meaningful way to stand with us.
But we want to be clear about something important.
Biblical giving is meant to be willing, thoughtful, and sincere—not compelled by guilt.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver.
But if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture more deeply, return to prayer, confront a hidden compromise, or draw nearer to Christ, consider helping us continue that work.
These items are simply expressions of gratitude and tools that may encourage faith-centered living. The real value of discipleship is never measured by merchandise or discounts.
These resources are intended to help believers deepen their understanding of Scripture, strengthen their prayer lives, and continue growing in Jesus Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your comments matter.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
And when you are able to give financially, that support can also help make the ministry's continued work possible.
Our goal is not to build a community impressed with Gospel Warrior.
It is to build a community increasingly devoted to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest testimony of any Christian ministry is not how many people admire its content.
It is whether people are being faithfully directed toward the Savior.
And that brings us back to the man in Corinth.
A man who crossed a forbidden boundary.
A congregation that responded with pride instead of grief.
An apostle who refused to pretend that sin was harmless.
And a Savior whose sacrifice stood at the center of Paul's appeal.
The ancient commandment was not meaningless.
The scandal was not trivial.
The call to holiness was not optional.
But neither was the message of redemption absent.
The same Gospel that exposes sin announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
The same Lord who commands repentance welcomes those who turn to Him.
And the same grace that rescues us from condemnation teaches us to walk in a different direction.
Maybe that is the message you needed today.
Not that your past was harmless.
Not that every choice you made was right.
Not that the wounds you caused or suffered can be dismissed with a religious phrase.
But that your story does not have to end in the darkness where sin brought you.
Come to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Turn from what He calls sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His mercy.
And keep walking with Him, one faithful step at a time.
Because the most astonishing part of the Gospel is not that God found people who had never fallen.
It is that the holy Son of God came to save sinners.
The scandal may explain how you fell, but it does not have the authority to decide who you become in Christ.
